source_title: Figure 1.6 The Three States of Matter
source_caption: Solids have a defined shape and volume. Liquids have a fixed volume but flow to assume the shape of their containers. Gases completely fill their containers, regardless of volume.
replacement_brief: Three panels showing fixed solid shape, liquid taking the vessel shape, and gas filling different vessel volumes. Label properties; add particle insets.

source_title: Figure 1.7 A Heterogeneous Mixture
source_caption: Under a microscope, whole milk is actually a heterogeneous mixture composed of globules of fat and protein dispersed in water.
replacement_brief: Pair a milk sample with a licensed micrograph of milk fat globules. A particle schematic is a fallback, explicitly identified as schematic.
editorial_review: Do not present an invented illustration as microscopy.

source_title: Figure 1.8 The Distillation of a Solution of Table Salt in Water
source_caption: The solution of salt in water is heated in the distilling flask until it boils. The resulting vapor is enriched in the more volatile component (water), which condenses to a liquid in the cold condenser and is then collected in the receiving flask.
replacement_brief: Adapt an open SVG or draw a boiling flask, condenser with coolant inlet/outlet, and receiving flask. Mark water vapor and distillate, with nonvolatile salt remaining behind.

source_title: Figure 1.9 The Crystallization of Sodium Acetate from a Concentrated Solution of Sodium Acetate in Water
source_caption: The addition of a small “seed” crystal (a) causes the compound to form white crystals, which grow and eventually occupy most of the flask (b).
replacement_brief: Find a before/after sequence showing seeding of a supersaturated sodium acetate solution and crystal growth in the same vessel.
editorial_review: Match the seeding sequence; an unrelated mineral crystal is insufficient.

source_title: Figure 1.16 A Gas Discharge Tube Producing Cathode Rays
source_caption: When a high voltage is applied to a gas contained at low pressure in a gas discharge tube, electricity flows through the gas, and energy is emitted in the form of light.
replacement_brief: Draw a low-pressure tube, labeled cathode/anode, high-voltage supply, and light emission. Distinguish electron travel from emitted light.

source_title: Figure 2.9 Loss of Water from a Hydrate with Heating
source_caption: When blue CuSO 4 ·5H 2 O is heated, two molecules of water are lost at 30°C, two more at 110°C, and the last at 250°C to give white CuSO 4 .
replacement_brief: Pair blue copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate with white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate; add a heating arrow and formula labels.
editorial_review: Check the source temperature/staged-dehydration claims before adding numerical labels.

source_caption: Sodium. The fourth most abundant alkali metal on Earth, sodium is a highly reactive element that is never found free in nature. When heated to 250°C, it bursts into flames if exposed to air.
replacement_brief: Find an openly licensed sodium specimen photograph; retain only caption statements supported by the selected image.

source_title: Figure 3.1 Samples of 1 Mol of Some Common Substances
replacement_brief: Make a labeled panel of representative substances with one-mole masses and particle types: atoms, molecules, or formula units.
editorial_review: Original specimen identities and amounts are not recoverable from the missing pixels. Select documented examples and revise the caption; do not imply sample volumes are measured.

source_title: Figure 3.7 An Ammonium Dichromate Volcano: Change during a Chemical Reaction
source_caption: The starting material (left) is solid ammonium dichromate. A chemical reaction (right) transforms it to solid chromium(III) oxide, depicted showing a portion of its chained structure, nitrogen gas, and water vapor. (In addition, energy in the form of heat and light is released.) During the reaction, the distribution of atoms changes, but the number of atoms of each element does not change. Because the numbers of each type of atom are the same in the reactants and the products, the chemical equation is balanced.
replacement_brief: Show orange ammonium dichromate becoming green chromium(III) oxide, N2, and water vapor; include the balanced equation and atom counts.
editorial_review: Describe any oxide network sketch as schematic unless supported by structural data.

source_title: Figure 3.9 An Example of a Combustion Reaction
source_caption: The wax in a candle is a high-molecular-mass hydrocarbon, which produces gaseous carbon dioxide and water vapor in a combustion reaction. When the candle is allowed to burn inside a flask, drops of water, one of the products of combustion, condense at the top of the inner surface of the flask.
replacement_brief: Show a burning candle inside a flask, water droplets on cooler glass, and carbon dioxide/water products.

source_caption: Crystalline galena (a) and a sample of lead (b). Pure lead is soft enough to be shaped easily with a hammer, unlike the brittle mineral galena, the main ore of lead.
replacement_brief: Use two licensed specimen photographs showing crystalline galena and metallic lead, with distinct labels.

source_caption: AgCl(s) precipitates when solutions of AgNO 3 (aq) and NaCl(aq) are mixed. NaNO 3 (aq) is in solution as Na + and NO 3 − ions.
replacement_brief: Draw AgNO3 and NaCl solutions forming white AgCl solid, with Na+ and nitrate remaining in solution; conserve ions.

source_caption: The reaction of mercury(II) acetate with sodium iodide. When colorless aqueous solutions of each reactant are mixed, they produce a red precipitate, mercury(II) iodide, which is the result of an exchange reaction.
replacement_brief: Find a licensed image of red mercury(II) iodide precipitation; a clearly labeled reaction schematic is the fallback.
editorial_review: Do not substitute a different red precipitate under the existing caption.

source_title: Figure 4.4 The Effect of Ions on the Electrical Conductivity of Water
source_caption: An electrical current will flow and light the bulb only if the solution contains ions. (a) Pure water or an aqueous solution of a nonelectrolyte allows almost no current to flow, and the bulb does not light. (b) A weak electrolyte produces a few ions, allowing some current to flow and the bulb to glow dimly. (c) A strong electrolyte produces many ions, allowing more current to flow and the bulb to shine brightly.
replacement_brief: Draw the same circuit in three panels: nonelectrolyte, weak electrolyte, strong electrolyte. Show particle speciation and off/dim/bright lamp states.
editorial_review: Use controlled concentrations and qualitative brightness; avoid implying that every strong electrolyte has the same conductivity.

source_caption: A Breathalyzer ampul before (a) and after (b) ethanol is added. When a measured volume of a suspect’s breath is bubbled through the solution, the ethanol is oxidized to acetic acid, and the solution changes color from yellow-orange to green. The intensity of the green color indicates the amount of ethanol in the sample.
replacement_brief: Show the dichromate-based test before/after ethanol oxidation, with orange/yellow and green solutions and a labeled reaction arrow.
editorial_review: Identify this as a schematic of the historical test, rather than a photograph or a calibration standard.

source_title: Figure 4.11 What Happens at the Molecular Level When Solutions of AgNO 3 and K 2 Cr 2 O 7 Are Mixed
source_caption: The Ag + and Cr 2 O 7 2− ions form a red precipitate of solid Ag 2 Cr 2 O 7 , while the K + and NO 3 − ions remain in solution. (Water molecules are omitted from molecular views of the solutions for clarity.)
replacement_brief: Show molecular-level mixing of AgNO3 and K2Cr2O7, red Ag2Cr2O7 solid, and spectator K+/NO3-; preserve intact polyatomic ions and stoichiometry.

source_caption: An x-ray of the digestive organs of a patient who has swallowed a “barium milkshake.” A barium milkshake is a suspension of very fine BaSO 4 particles in water; the high atomic mass of barium makes it opaque to x-rays.
replacement_brief: Find an explicitly reusable barium-contrast radiograph illustrating the digestive tract.
editorial_review: A synthetic radiograph would not provide observational evidence; an anatomical diagram would need a different caption.

source_caption: Darkening of silver bromide crystals by exposure to light. The top image shows AgBr before exposure to light, and the bottom image after exposure.
replacement_brief: Find a licensed before/after image of silver bromide exposed to light, or commission an original documented photograph.
editorial_review: Match AgBr rather than silently substituting AgCl.

source_title: Figure 4.14 The Reaction of Dilute Aqueous HNO 3 with a Solution of Na 2 CO 3
source_caption: Note the vigorous formation of gaseous CO 2 .
replacement_brief: Draw dilute nitric acid added to sodium carbonate solution with CO2 bubbles and the corresponding reaction labels.

source_title: Figure 4.16 Two Ways of Measuring the pH of a Solution: pH Paper and a pH Meter
source_caption: Note that both show that the pH is 1.7, but the pH meter gives a more precise value.
replacement_brief: Compare an indicator-strip color match with a digital meter reading 1.7, using clear labels about approximate versus finer numerical readings.
editorial_review: Review the source claim that pH paper also reads exactly 1.7; do not invent a commercial strip calibration.

source_title: Figure 4.21 The Single-Displacement Reaction of Metallic Copper with a Solution of Silver Nitrate
source_caption: When a copper coil is placed in a solution of silver nitrate, silver ions are reduced to metallic silver on the copper surface, and some of the copper metal dissolves. Note the formation of a metallic silver precipitate on the copper coil and a blue color in the surrounding solution due to the presence of aqueous Cu 2+ ions. (Water molecules and nitrate ions have been omitted from molecular views of the solution for clarity.)
replacement_brief: Combine a licensed copper/silver-nitrate reaction photograph with a new particle diagram showing Ag deposition and Cu2+ formation. A full schematic can replace the photograph if needed.

source_title: Figure 4.23 The Titration of Oxalic Acid with Permanganate
source_caption: As small volumes of permanganate solution are added to the oxalate solution, a transient purple color appears and then disappears as the permanganate is consumed (a). As more permanganate is added, eventually all the oxalate is oxidized, and a faint purple color from the presence of excess permanganate appears, marking the endpoint (b).
replacement_brief: Show transient purple titrant color disappearing before the endpoint, and persistent faint color at the endpoint; include a buret and panel labels.
editorial_review: Use the color stated in the reviewed caption, and distinguish a transient local plume from the final mixed solution.

source_title: Figure 4.24 The Titration of Ascorbic Acid with a Solution of NaOH
source_caption: The solution, containing bromothymol blue as an indicator, is initially yellow (a). The addition of a trace excess of NaOH causes the solution to turn green at the endpoint (b) and then blue.
replacement_brief: Show bromothymol blue changing from yellow through green at the endpoint to blue with excess NaOH, with buret and solution labels.

source_title: Figure 5.12 An Instant Hot Pack Based on the Crystallization of Sodium Acetate
source_caption: The hot pack is at room temperature prior to agitation (left). Because the sodium acetate is in solution, you can see the metal disc inside the pack. After the hot pack has been agitated, the sodium acetate crystallizes (right) to release heat. Because of the mass of white sodium acetate that has crystallized, the metal disc is no longer visible.
replacement_brief: Use before/after photographs, potentially frames from a licensed activation video, showing a clear pack becoming crystalline and opaque.
editorial_review: Verify that the selected pack actually shows the disc visibility described in the caption, or rewrite that detail.

source_caption: The noble gases. Helium, neon, argon, krypton, and xenon, all monatomic elements, are five of the six known noble gases. When atoms of these gases are excited by the flow of electrons in the discharge tubes, they emit photons of visible light in their characteristic spectral colors. All noble gases have the maximum number of electrons possible in their outer shell (2 for helium, 8 for all others), so they do not form chemical compounds easily.
replacement_brief: Find a licensed composite or consistent photographs of labeled He, Ne, Ar, Kr, and Xe discharge tubes.
editorial_review: Do not assign tube colors or identities from appearance alone.

source_title: Figure 6.9 The Emission of Light by Hydrogen Atoms
source_caption: (a) A sample of excited hydrogen atoms emits a characteristic red light. (b) When the light emitted by a sample of excited hydrogen atoms is split into its component wavelengths by a prism, four characteristic violet, blue, green, and red emission lines can be observed, the most intense of which is at 656 nm.
replacement_brief: Pair a licensed hydrogen discharge-tube photograph with an accurately positioned Balmer-line SVG. A labeled apparatus schematic is a fallback for the photograph.
editorial_review: Use documented wavelengths and distinguish line intensity from display color.

source_title: Figure 6.13 The Emission Spectra of Elements Compared with Hydrogen
source_caption: These images show (a) hydrogen gas, which is atomized to hydrogen atoms in the discharge tube; (b) neon; and (c) mercury.
replacement_brief: Draw emission-line strips for hydrogen, neon, and mercury on a shared wavelength scale, based on documented atomic spectral data.
editorial_review: Do not invent spectral lines or use decorative gradients as data.

source_caption: Potassium burning. A piece of potassium dropped in a beaker of water will burn as it skips across the top of the water.
replacement_brief: Find an openly licensed photograph or video frame of the potassium-water reaction.
editorial_review: Match the metal identity; a sodium-water photograph is not interchangeable.

source_caption: Carbon and silicon bonding. Both the group 14 elements carbon and silicon form bonds with oxygen, but how they form those bonds results in a vast difference in physical properties. Because of its simple molecular bond, carbon dioxide is a gas that exists as a volatile molecular solid, known as “dry ice,” at temperatures of −78°C and below. Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure, whose strong bonds in three dimensions make it a hard, high-melting-point solid, such as quartz.
replacement_brief: Contrast discrete CO2 molecules in dry ice with an extended SiO2 covalent network, labeled with their different physical properties.
editorial_review: Distinguish intramolecular CO2 bonds from intermolecular forces in dry ice.

source_title: Figure 9.27 Liquid O 2 Suspended between the Poles of a Magnet
source_caption: Because the O 2 molecule has two unpaired electrons, it is paramagnetic. Consequently, it is attracted into a magnetic field, which allows it to remain suspended between the poles of a powerful magnet until it evaporates.
replacement_brief: Use a licensed photograph or higher-resolution source-video frame showing liquid oxygen held between magnetic poles.
editorial_review: The identified Commons stills are only about 300 pixels wide; inspect legibility before selecting.
candidate_status: description/license checked; visual and scientific acceptance pending

source_title: Figure 10.15 The Diffusion of Gaseous Molecules
source_caption: When open containers of aqueous NH 3 and HCl are placed near each other in a draft-free environment, molecules of the two substances diffuse, collide, and react to produce white fumes of solid ammonium chloride (NH 4 Cl).
replacement_brief: Show separate open ammonia and hydrochloric-acid containers, diffusion paths, and a white NH4Cl aerosol where gases meet.
editorial_review: Distinguish dissolved source reagents, gaseous reactants, and solid aerosol product.

source_title: Figure 10.16 A Simple Experiment to Measure the Relative Rates of the Diffusion of Two Gases
source_caption: Cotton balls containing aqueous NH 3 (left) and HCl (right) are placed a measured distance apart in a draft-free environment, and the position at which white fumes of NH 4 Cl first appear is noted. The puff of white NH 4 Cl forms much closer to the HCl-containing ball than to the NH 3 -containing ball. The left edge of the white puff marks where the reaction was first observed. The position of the white puff (18.8 − 3.3 = 15.5 cm from the NH 3 , 28.0 − 18.8 = 9.2 cm from the HCl, giving a ratio of distances of 15.5/9.2 = 1.7) is approximately the location predicted by Graham’s law based on the square root of the inverse ratio of the molar masses of the reactants (1.47).
replacement_brief: Draw cotton sources and a ruler with source positions at 3.3 and 28.0 cm and the observed cloud edge at 18.8 cm; label 15.5 cm, 9.2 cm, and observed ratio about 1.7.
editorial_review: Keep the observed 1.7 ratio distinct from the theoretical 1.47 ratio. Review the nearby equation that labels NH4Cl as gas instead of solid aerosol.

source_title: Figure 11.1 Molecular Diffusion in a Liquid
source_caption: A drop of an aqueous solution containing a marker dye is added to a larger volume of water. As it diffuses, the color of the dye becomes fainter at the edges.
replacement_brief: Draw a clearly identified qualitative time sequence showing a dye drop dispersing through water, with no imposed current or stirring.
editorial_review: Do not imply measured time intervals or a quantitative concentration profile.

source_title: Figure 11.10 The Effects of the High Surface Tension of Liquid Water
source_caption: (a) A paper clip can “float” on water because of surface tension. (b) Surface tension also allows insects such as this water strider to “walk on water.”
replacement_brief: Find licensed photographs of a supported paper clip and a water strider, preserving the two examples.

source_title: Figure 11.11 The Phenomenon of Capillary Action
source_caption: When a glass capillary is placed in liquid water, water rises up into the capillary. The smaller the diameter of the capillary, the higher the water rises. The height of the water does not depend on the angle at which the capillary is tilted.
replacement_brief: Show water rising higher in narrower glass capillaries, and a tilted capillary with the same vertical rise as a comparable vertical tube.

source_title: Figure 11.12 The Effects of Capillary Action
source_caption: (a) This drawing illustrates the shape of the meniscus and the relative height of a mercury column when a glass capillary is put into liquid mercury. The meniscus is convex and the surface of the liquid inside the tube is lower than the level of the liquid outside the tube. (b) Because water adheres strongly to the polar surface of glass, it has a concave meniscus, whereas mercury, which does not adhere to the glass, has a convex meniscus.

source_title: Figure 11.18 The Sublimation of Solid Iodine
source_caption: When solid iodine is heated at ordinary atmospheric pressure, it sublimes. When the I 2 vapor comes in contact with a cold surface, it deposits I 2 crystals.
replacement_brief: Find a licensed photograph showing iodine vapor and deposition of iodine crystals on a cold surface.
editorial_review: Do not replace iodine with a different subliming substance under this caption.

source_title: Figure 11.25 Cholesteryl Benzoate
source_caption: (a) When the temperature is greater than 179°C, the substance is an isotropic liquid through which images can be seen. (b) When the temperature is between 145°C and 179°C, the substance is in the cholesteric liquid crystalline phase and is an opaque, milky liquid.
replacement_brief: Find a licensed matched pair for transparent isotropic liquid above 179 C and milky cholesteric phase at 145-179 C.
editorial_review: Generic liquid-crystal photographs will not establish the named substance or temperature ranges; use a schematic with revised caption if no match is available.

source_title: Figure 13.5 Immiscible Liquids
source_caption: Water is immiscible with both CCl 4 and hexane. When all three liquids are mixed, they separate into three distinct layers. Because water is less dense than CCl 4 , the water layer floats on the CCl 4 . In contrast, hexane is less dense than water, so the hexane floats on the water layer. Because I 2 is intensely purple and quite soluble in both CCl 4 and hexane, but insoluble in water, a small amount of I 2 has been added to help identify the hexane and CCl 4 layers.
replacement_brief: After chemistry review, draw the correct phase arrangement with solvent names, densities/order, and iodine distribution. Consider two separate binary-mixture panels.
editorial_review: The caption asserts three stable layers of water, CCl4, and hexane. Verify mutual miscibility of the two organic solvents before depicting this; do not recreate the claim blindly.

source_title: Figure 13.8 Effect of a Crown Ether on the Solubility of KMnO 4 in Isopropanol (2-Propanol)
source_caption: (a) Normally KMnO 4 , which is intensely purple, is completely insoluble in isopropanol, which has a relatively low dielectric constant. (b) In the presence of a small amount of 18-crown-6, KMnO 4 dissolves in isopropanol, as shown by the reddish-purple color caused by permanganate ions in solution.
replacement_brief: Show KMnO4 before/after addition of 18-crown-6 in isopropanol, with K+ binding and a qualitative purple solution indicator.

source_title: Figure 13.22 Tyndall Effect, the Scattering of Light by Colloids
source_caption: Both cylinders contain a solution of red food coloring in water, but a small amount of gelatin has been added to the cylinder on the right to form a colloidal suspension of gelatin particles. The beam of light goes straight through the true solution on the left, but the light beam is scattered by the colloid on the right.
replacement_brief: Show the same side-illuminating beam in true solution and gelatin colloid, with side scattering visible only for the colloid.
editorial_review: A generic image of sunbeams is not a substitute for the controlled liquid comparison.

source_title: Figure 14.1 The Effect of Concentration on Reaction Rates
source_caption: Mixing sucrose with dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker (a, right) produces a simple solution. Mixing the same amount of sucrose with concentrated sulfuric acid (a, left) results in a dramatic reaction (b) that eventually produces a column of black porous graphite (c) and an intense smell of burning sugar.
replacement_brief: Find a licensed sequence contrasting dilute acid with the concentrated sulfuric-acid/sucrose reaction and its black carbonaceous product.
editorial_review: Verify the caption description of the product as graphite before labeling a replacement.

source_title: Figure 14.2 The Effect of Temperature on Reaction Rates
source_caption: At high temperature, the reaction that produces light in a chemiluminescent light stick occurs more rapidly, producing more photons of light per unit time. Consequently, the light glows brighter in hot water (left) than in ice water (right).
replacement_brief: Find a matched photograph of identical chemiluminescent sticks in hot versus ice water, with explicit temperature-condition labels.
editorial_review: Brightness depends on exposure as well as reaction rate; avoid fabricated quantitative brightness comparisons.

source_title: Figure 14.3 The Effect of Surface Area on Reaction Rates
source_caption: A pile of flour is only scorched by a flame (right), but when the same flour is sprayed into the flame, it burns rapidly (left).
replacement_brief: Contrast bulk flour with dispersed flour particles exposed to a flame, using a schematic to explain increased accessible surface area.
editorial_review: Label this as a conceptual comparison, not a recorded experiment.

source_title: Figure 14.4 The Effect of Catalysts on Reaction Rates
source_caption: A solution of hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) decomposes in water so slowly that the change is not noticeable (left). Iodide ion acts as a catalyst for the decomposition of H 2 O 2 , producing oxygen gas. The solution turns brown because of the reaction of H 2 O 2 with I − , which generates small amounts of I 3 − (center). The enzyme catalase is about 3 billion times more effective than iodide as a catalyst. Even in the presence of very small amounts of enzyme, the decomposition is vigorous (right).
replacement_brief: Draw control, iodide, and catalase panels, with qualitative O2 evolution and explanatory catalyst labels.
editorial_review: Do not turn the source relative-effectiveness claim into measured bubble counts or a numerical rate chart without evidence.

source_title: Figure 15.1 The N 2 O(g) ⇌ 2 NO 2 (g) System at Different Temperatures
source_caption: (left) At dry ice temperature (−78.4°C), the system contains essentially pure solid N 2 O 4 , which is colorless. (center) As the system is warmed above the melting point of N 2 O 4 (−9.3°C), the N 2 O 4 melts and then evaporates, and some of the vapor dissociates to red-brown NO 2 . (right) Eventually the sample reaches room temperature, and a mixture of gaseous N 2 O 4 and NO 2 is present. The composition of the mixture and hence the color do not change further with time: the system has reached equilibrium at the new temperature.
replacement_brief: Show cold colorless N2O4, warming/evaporation, and the room-temperature brown equilibrium mixture; label phases and the balanced equilibrium.
editorial_review: The source figure heading and Equation 15.1 use N2O where the surrounding text specifies N2O4. Correct and document this before producing the diagram.

source_title: Figure 15.12 The Effect of Changing the Volume (and Thus the Pressure) of an Equilibrium Mixture of N 2 O 4 and NO 2 at Constant Temperature
source_caption: (a) The syringe with a total volume of 15 mL contains an equilibrium mixture of N 2 O 4 and NO 2 ; the red-brown color is proportional to the NO 2 concentration. (b) If the volume is rapidly decreased by a factor of 2 to 7.5 mL, the initial effect is to double the concentrations of all species present, including NO 2 . Hence the color becomes more intense. (c) With time, the system adjusts its composition in response to the stress as predicted by Le Châtelier’s principle, forming colorless N 2 O 4 at the expense of red-brown NO 2 , which decreases the intensity of the color of the mixture.
replacement_brief: Draw three syringe states: 15 mL equilibrium, immediate compression to 7.5 mL with darker color, then relaxation toward N2O4.
editorial_review: Keep immediate concentration changes distinct from the later equilibrium shift; do not imply the final color must be lighter than the original state.

source_title: Figure 15.13 The Effect of Temperature on the Equilibrium between Gaseous N 2 O 4 and NO 2
source_caption: (center) A tube containing a mixture of N 2 O 4 and NO 2 in the same proportion at room temperature is red-brown due to the NO 2 present. (left) Immersing the tube in ice water causes the mixture to become lighter in color due to a shift in the equilibrium composition toward colorless N 2 O 4 . (right) In contrast, immersing the same tube in boiling water causes the mixture to become darker due to a shift in the equilibrium composition toward the highly colored NO 2 .
replacement_brief: Draw equal-volume N2O4/NO2 samples in cold, room-temperature, and hot conditions, with lighter-to-darker qualitative colors and shift arrows.

source_caption: Indicators are used to monitor changes in pH. The pH of a solution can be monitored using an acid–base indicator, a substance that undergoes a color change within a specific pH range that is characteristic of that indicator. The color changes for seven commonly used indicators over a pH range of 1–10 are shown here.
replacement_brief: Create seven labeled indicator color bars over pH 1-10, using verified indicator identities and transition ranges.
editorial_review: The missing image contained the original seven identities. Recover them from another documented source or select from surviving Figure 16.23 and revise the caption.

source_title: Figure 16.22 Naturally Occurring pH Indicators in Red Cabbage Juice
source_caption: Red cabbage juice contains a mixture of substances whose color depends on the pH. Each test tube contains a solution of red cabbage juice in water, but the pH of the solutions varies from pH = 2.0 (far left) to pH = 11.0 (far right). At pH = 7.0, the solution is blue.
replacement_brief: Use a licensed cabbage-juice pH series; preserve only pH values actually documented by the photographer.
editorial_review: The candidates do not establish the original exact pH=2 to pH=11 sequence or the pH=7 tube. Revise the caption rather than assigning unsupported values.

source_title: Figure 16.25 pH Paper
source_caption: pH paper contains a set of indicators that change color at different pH values. The approximate pH of a solution can be determined by simply dipping a paper strip into the solution and comparing the color to the standards provided.
replacement_brief: Find a licensed photograph of indicator strips with their matching reference chart.
editorial_review: Do not combine a strip with an unrelated manufacturer color chart.

source_caption: A crystal of calcite (CaCO 3 ), illustrating the phenomenon of double refraction. When a transparent crystal of calcite is placed over a page, we see two images of the letters.
replacement_brief: Use a licensed calcite-rhomb photograph showing a doubled underlying image or line.

source_title: Figure 17.4 The Formation of Complex Ions
source_caption: An aqueous solution of CuSO 4 consists of hydrated Cu 2+ ions in the form of pale blue [Cu(H 2 O) 6 ] 2+ (left). The addition of aqueous ammonia to the solution results in the formation of the intensely blue-violet [Cu(NH 3 ) 4 (H 2 O) 2 ] 2+ ions, usually written as [Cu(NH 3 ) 4 ] 2+ ion (right) because ammonia, a stronger base than H 2 O, replaces water molecules from the hydrated Cu 2+ ion.
replacement_brief: Show pale-blue hydrated Cu2+ becoming the deep-blue ammonia complex; label coordination and ligand substitution.
editorial_review: Use schematic colors, with the retained two axial water ligands described consistently.

source_title: Figure 17.9 Chromium(III) Hydroxide [Cr(OH) 3 or Cr 2 O 3 ·3H 2 O] Is an Example of an Amphoteric Oxide
source_caption: All three beakers originally contained a suspension of brownish purple Cr(OH) 3 (s) (center). When concentrated acid (6 M H 2 SO 4 ) was added to the beaker on the left, Cr(OH) 3 dissolved to produce violet [Cr(H 2 O) 6 ] 3+ ions and water. The addition of concentrated base (6 M NaOH) to the beaker on the right caused Cr(OH) 3 to dissolve, producing green [Cr(OH) 4 ] − ions.
replacement_brief: Draw the central Cr(OH)3 suspension with acid and base branches giving the labeled dissolved complexes.
editorial_review: Review species and experimental conditions before committing to exact colors.

source_title: Figure 17.11 The Separation of Metal Ions from Group 1 Using Qualitative Analysis
source_caption: In (a), the cations of group 1 precipitate when HCl(aq) is added to a solution containing a mixture of cations. (b) When a small amount of Na 2 CrO 4 solution is added to a sample containing Pb 2+ ions in water, a bright yellow precipitate of PbCrO 4 forms. (c) Adding aqueous ammonia to a second portion of the solid sample produces a black solid that is a mixture of finely divided metallic mercury, an insoluble mercury(II) compound [Hg(NH 2 )Cl], and a stable [Ag(NH 3 ) 2 ] + (aq) complex. (d) The presence of Ag + is detected by decanting the solution from the precipitated mercury and mercury complex and adding hydrochloric acid to the decanted solution, which causes AgCl to precipitate.
replacement_brief: Create a separation flowchart and small vessel panels for HCl precipitation, PbCrO4 confirmation, ammonia treatment, and AgCl reprecipitation.
editorial_review: Preserve the actual Ag/Pb/Hg reagents, phases, and sequence; do not infer extra test associations.

source_title: Figure 18.6 An Endothermic Reaction
source_caption: The reaction of barium hydroxide with ammonium thiocyanate is spontaneous but highly endothermic, so water, one product of the reaction, quickly freezes into slush. When water is placed on a block of wood under the flask, the highly endothermic reaction that takes place in the flask freezes water that has been placed under the beaker, so the flask becomes frozen to the wood.
replacement_brief: Draw the reaction flask on wet wood, heat flowing into the flask, and water freezing at the contact; label the reaction as endothermic and spontaneous under the stated conditions.

source_title: Figure 18.7 Illustrating Low- and High-Entropy States with a Deck of Playing Cards
